citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Consider an actual smooth complex rank-$m$ strip bundle, totally real horizontal boundary subbundles, specified end frames identifying these subbundles with $\mathbb R^m,i\mathbb R^m$, and a smooth real first-order operator with Cauchy–Riemann symbol and exact expression $\partial_s+i\partial_t$ in those frames outside a compact set. Its index means the real Fredholm index before source translation, on fixed-end $H^{q+1}\to H^q$ spaces, for an integer $q\ge0$.

Take a compact strip rectangle $Q$ containing the nonconstant part. Complete the horizontal boundary subbundles to a totally real loop along $\partial Q$ using the vertical end caps
$$L_\pm(t)=\tau_\pm e^{i\pi\rho(t)/2}\mathbb R^m,$$
where $\rho:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ is smooth, zero near zero, one near one, and increases from zero to one. The boundary orientation is that induced by $ds\wedge dt$. In any smooth global complex frame on $Q$, a local real basis $v_1,\ldots,v_m$ of this loop defines
$$\zeta=\frac{(\det_{\mathbb C}(v_1,\ldots,v_m))^2}{|\det_{\mathbb C}(v_1,\ldots,v_m)|^2}\in S^1.$$
These local expressions agree on overlaps. Its integer winding $M$ is independent of real bases, global complex frame, sufficiently large rectangle, and cap cutoff $\rho$, and
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}P=M.$$
The equality also holds with smooth two-sided weights below the end spectral gap $\pi/2$. This specifies actual caps and signs, rather than defining an unexplained topological index.

The following finite-dimensional excision and model calculations hold with the same squared determinant convention.

* Direct sums add $M$. Gluing two such strip problems with matching product end frames and operators exactly constant near the cut adds their actual real indices. This is a statement about the glued linear boundary problem.
* On a rectangle with finitely many disjoint round interior disks removed, suppose a continuous totally real subbundle in a trivial complex bundle is defined on the remaining compact surface. Then the determinant winding along the outer boundary is the sum of its windings along the positively counterclockwise hole circles. It suffices that the bundle be smooth near the boundary circles; for a smooth bundle the local windings can be computed by the following models.
* For the symmetric-coordinate map $q(z_1,z_2)=(z_1+z_2,z_1z_2)$, transport the two real lines generated by the same nonzero constant $v\in\mathbb C$ along $z_1=-\sqrt w,z_2=\sqrt w$, $w$ traversing a small counterclockwise circle. Their image under $dq$ has squared determinant winding $+1$. More generally an order-$r$ source-cover model consisting of the $r$ roots of $w$, with the same constant source vector on each sheet and elementary symmetric target coordinates, has winding $r-1$.
* A scalar target map $f(z)=z^{r+1}$, on a sheet unbranched over the parameter disk, sends a nonzero constant real direction to a line of squared phase winding $2r$ along a positive source circle.
* For two graph branches $(z,Az),(z,Bz)$ in $\mathbb C\times\mathbb C$, with $A,B:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ real linear invertible and $A-B$ invertible, choose source directions $A^{-1}v,B^{-1}v$ for a fixed nonzero $v\in\mathbb C$. Push their target directions to the symmetric coordinates of $Az,Bz$. The resulting two-plane has squared determinant winding $2\operatorname{sign}\det_{\mathbb R}(A-B)$. This sign equals the oriented intersection sign of the two graph sheets, both oriented by their $z$ coordinate and the product oriented by base then target.
* A scalar source direction winding $k$ on an otherwise nonsingular sheet contributes $2k$ to the squared determinant winding. Extra fixed nonzero product directions change none of these local contributions.

These assertions do not identify the domain Euler measure or corner multiplicities of an arbitrary Whitney class. In particular, no representativity theorem, collapsed-tube calculation, corner rounding formula, or branched-cover Euler identity is included.

Let $M$ be a compact oriented surface with supplied finite smooth triangle data, with circular interior and interval boundary links. Let $E\to M\times[0,1]$ be a complex line bundle and $s$ a continuous section, smooth on each end slice. Assume $s$ is nonzero on $\partial M\times[0,1]$, and that $s_0,s_1$ have finitely many isolated zeros, none on the vertices or edges of the supplied triangles. At an isolated zero its index is the winding of its coordinate value in any local complex frame along a small positive coordinate circle. Then
$$\sum_{s_0(p)=0}\operatorname{ind}_p(s_0)=\sum_{s_1(p)=0}\operatorname{ind}_p(s_1).$$
Intermediate zero sets may be nonisolated. No genericity of the family is assumed.

Consequently, let $Z$ be a closed oriented embedded codimension-two submanifold without boundary in an oriented smooth manifold $W$, with a supplied metric oriented normal disk tube, and let $F:M\times[0,1]\to W$ be a continuous homotopy smooth on the end slices. Assume its boundary image avoids $Z$ for every parameter and its end slices have finitely many isolated intersections with $Z$ away from the triangle edges. The algebraic end intersection sums are equal. Here a local intersection number is the winding of the oriented normal coordinate of $F$ around a small source circle; at a transverse intersection it is the usual sign of the induced isomorphism from the oriented source tangent plane to the oriented normal plane of $Z$. No compactness assertion for a noncompact homotopy is implicit: this statement uses the compact parameterized surface $M\times[0,1]$.

The following boundary version is also valid with explicit extra data. Suppose the relative problem has a supplied smooth reflection double, on which the doubled two surfaces and homotopy meet the preceding hypotheses. Require that reflection interchange the two interior copies and preserve their local intersection signs, and that every boundary intersection have just one doubled local representative, with the indicated sign. Then the conserved quantity on one copy is
$$I=\sum_{\text{interior intersections}}\operatorname{sign}+\frac12\sum_{\text{boundary intersections}}\operatorname{sign},$$
or the same expression with isolated local multiplicities. The assertion includes no construction of a global reflection double for arbitrary boundary data.

An explicit local model realizes the half weight. In $\mathbb C_a\times\mathbb C_b$ with complex product orientation, take the graph $G=\{(z^{r+1},z):z\in\mathbb C\}$ and its translate $G_\varepsilon=\{(z^{r+1},z+\varepsilon):z\in\mathbb C\}$ for $r\ge0$ and real $\varepsilon\ne0$. Their finite intersections have total positive multiplicity $r$. Restricting both graphs to $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, with intersections on the real boundary counted by one half, gives total $r/2$. These local counts concern a neighborhood containing all those roots, and hence may be used in a sufficiently small translated power-branch model.

All assertions above require no choice principle. The finite tube and any reflection double are hypotheses, not unproved consequences about a general Whitney or cylindrical representative.

derivations.claim: Around an ordered tuple choose pairwise disjoint complex coordinate disks about its distinct support points, using the SAME coordinate for every factor with that support. Group its factors by these disks. On their product the target chart consists of the elementary symmetric coefficients of each group. Consequently $dq$ is block diagonal, up to a fixed permutation of its columns, with the coefficient-map blocks in [F1]. In the corresponding tangent and determinant frames its determinant is $$c\prod_{\text{groups }I}\prod_{i<j\in I}(z_i-z_j),\qquad c\ne0.$$ Factors in different groups cannot coincide in this chart. This is an equality of holomorphic functions on the whole product chart, not merely on the distinct-root locus. Its coefficient $c$ is constant and nonzero, so there is no further zero at a higher collision. Each pair factor has multiplicity one as a divisor, even though several factors can vanish at one tuple. [F1, given, algebra]

We spell out the degree convention and its consequences. On a finite triangulated oriented closed surface choose a nonzero section $r$ of a line bundle along the entire edge graph. Such a section exists by the finite vertex and edge interpolation of [F2]. Frame the bundle on each closed face by its finite disk-frame construction. Define its degree as the sum over faces of the counterclockwise winding of the coordinate of $r$ on that face boundary. Changing a face frame changes its boundary winding by zero, since a nonzero disk function contracts radially. For another graph section $r'$, the ratio $r'/r$ is one nonzero function on the graph; its argument changes on every edge cancel between the two incident oriented faces. Thus the sum is independent of $r$ as well. Refining the supplied triangles does not change it, by the same cancellation on the new edges. Isomorphisms preserve this integer. Tensor products add it, by using tensor-product graph sections and face frames; a trivial line has degree zero. If a section has finitely many isolated zeros, choose graph perturbations missing those finitely many points and use that section for $r$. The finite zero excision in [F2] gives exactly the sum of its local indices, and refinements or graph perturbations do not change the degree by the cancellation just proved. The same computation works with a finite disk subdivision containing those small zero disks. [F2, construct, algebra]

Each pair diagonal has compatible local defining functions. Where two factors lie in one coordinate disk use $a_{ij}=z_i-z_j$; where their small coordinate disks are disjoint use the nonvanishing function one on that product chart. On overlapping coordinate disks a change $w=h(z)$ gives $$h(z_i)-h(z_j)=(z_i-z_j)u(z_i,z_j),$$ where $u$ is holomorphic and nonzero after shrinking about the diagonal: its extension on the diagonal is $h'(z_i)\ne0$. For example its power series is obtained by dividing the convergent series for the difference by $z_i-z_j$; away from the diagonal the ordinary quotient is already holomorphic. On intersections disjoint from the diagonal every relevant defining function is a unit. Thus products of the local pair definers give local functions $a_A$ for $R$ whose ratios are holomorphic units, including on overlaps containing higher collisions. Declare frames $e_A$ with transition $e_B=(a_A/a_B)e_A$. The expressions $a_Ae_A$ then agree and define a global holomorphic section $s_R$ of a line bundle $\mathcal O(R)$. The cocycle law is the literal cancellation of these ratios. Multiplying the pairwise transitions also identifies $\mathcal O(R)$ with the tensor product of their individual diagonal lines. No normal-crossing assumption on the union is used. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Write $L=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(\bigotimes_i p_i^*T\Sigma,q^*\det(TX))$ and $s=\det(dq)$. In a local frame $\ell_A$ of $L$, step1.1 writes $s=a_Au_A\ell_A$ with $u_A$ a holomorphic unit, after taking the defining product of step2.1 in the same charts. Define $\mathcal O(R)\to L$ there by $e_A\mapsto u_A\ell_A$. On the complement of the pair diagonals these maps are uniquely characterized by sending $s_R$ to $s$, and therefore agree on chart overlaps there. That complement is dense: finitely many coordinate equalities have empty interior. The maps agree everywhere by continuity, and are invertible since every $u_A$ is a unit. They give the claimed global holomorphic isomorphism. Tensoring by $\bigotimes_i p_i^*T\Sigma$ gives the displayed determinant identity. In particular this argument does not divide by a vanishing function without its proved holomorphic unit quotient. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Pull the bundle identity of step3.1 back by $F$ and apply the tensor-additivity of step1.2. Each pair line is the pullback of the diagonal line on $\Sigma\times\Sigma$, since their defining functions are the same coordinate differences; hence this gives precisely the asserted degree formula. At a coincidence its canonical section is locally $z(f_i)-z(f_j)$ in a nonvanishing frame. If that zero is transverse, its restriction to a small positive circle deforms through nonzero values to its invertible real derivative, whose winding is its orientation sign by [F2]. This proves the stated intersection interpretation when the zeros are isolated. If a section vanishes identically, step1.2 still defines the degree by a nonzero graph section, so the bundle identity and degree formula remain valid without a fictitious zero count. Finally for $m=1$ every product in step1.1 is empty and $dq$ is the identity; for $m=0$ all bundles are over a point and trivial. These checks prove the two edge cases and complete exactly the determinant and finite degree assertions, without a sphere-index or arbitrary-class conclusion. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

boundaries.evidence: Step 4.1 treats m=0 with all determinants trivial. See Statement and step 4.1.
Steps 1.1 and2.1 treat higher collisions by exact divisor products, not transverse zero counts. See Statement and step 4.1.
Steps 1.1 and4.1 treat m=1 with empty ramification divisor and identity quotient. See Statement and step 4.1.
Step 4.1 retains degree even for identically coincident component maps, without fictitious isolated zeros. See Statement and step 4.1.

boundaries.reason: The degree source is a closed surface and the line identity has no end conditions.

boundaries.evidence: Only finite local coordinates and supplied finite face frames are used; no AC surface classification or general transversality supplier. See Statement and step 4.1.
